question: How can two interrupting tempos make one movement?
intro: A quiet, singing Vivace is cut off after eight bars by an Adagio of forte arpeggios, and the two take turns for four minutes. Beethoven builds a sonata movement out of that quarrel between a bagatelle and a fantasia.

sections.label: Recapitulation · the Vivace material returns
sections.mNote: quiet Vivace material precedes the second Adagio

cues.title: A bagatelle and a fantasia
cues.text: A quiet, rapid Vivace melody in E major lasts eight bars. At bar 9 an Adagio espressivo interrupts with forte arpeggios and tense diminished-seventh harmony. The two ideas serve as first and second subjects of a sonata movement. The arpeggios sweep through both hands within the first half-minute.
cues.evidence: The Breitkopf score marks Adagio espressivo at bar 9; Wikipedia’s Op. 109 analysis, citing Charles Rosen, reads the two opening sections as first and second subjects. Detected attack density climbs from 1.8 to 4.0 per second by 0:30; no bar is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The cadence finally arrives
cues.text: Bar 8 never completes the expected cadence in B major, and bars 9–15 postpone it until bar 15. Around now the Adagio gives way to Tempo I, and the Vivace pace resumes.
cues.evidence: The cadence in bar 15 is documented in the sonata analysis cited above. The report shows boundaries at 0:34 (0.71) and 0:38 (0.70) where the texture reverts; bar 16 is not aligned to the audio.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A small new piece
cues.text: In April 1820 a conversation book mentions a “small new piece”. William Meredith identifies it with this movement, which the outline of a bagatelle broken by fantasia-like interludes supports. Beethoven’s secretary Franz Oliva is said to have suggested using it to open the sonata Schlesinger wanted.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Op. 109 article, genesis section, reports the April 1820 conversation-book entry (Meredith) and the Oliva suggestion, with its own citations: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven). The Oliva detail is stated as “allegedly” there and here.

cues.title: Near silence, then two swells
cues.text: Near 1:00 the sound all but vanishes, one of the quietest passages of the first half. It then swells twice, to loud windows at 1:20 and 1:35–1:40. The score stays in the Vivace tempo here, with legato lines, sf–p accents and a crescendo to loud octaves on its way to the return.
cues.evidence: Level is −38.2 dB at 1:00, −11.2 dB at 1:20 and −14.4 and −10.8 dB at 1:35 and 1:40; the loudest windows include 1:40, 1:20 and 1:35, with 2:15 and 2:35 also among the top five. The score (IMSLP #51804, printed pp. 98–99) shows legato, sfp accents, a crescendo and octaves marked f in this Tempo I stretch; they are not aligned to the recording, and the loud windows are not claimed to be a particular bar.

cues.title: A quiet stretch before the Adagio
cues.text: From about 1:54 the level falls away, from −17.6 dB at 1:50 to −29.9 dB by 2:05. In the score the Vivace material returns before the second Adagio, so this hush is a plausible place for it, but the report cannot confirm the bar.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 1:54 (novelty 0.54) follows the loud B-major-reading windows of 1:25–1:50 (r 0.87–0.95); level −23.3 dB at 1:55, −24.0 dB at 2:00 and −29.9 dB at 2:05. The score (IMSLP #51804, printed pp. 98–100) places Tempo I material before the second Adagio espressivo. Biamonti, quoted at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/Opus109/, has the first element return with ascending progressions that peak, then quickly diminish, restoring its original sweetness. The bar is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second Adagio
cues.text: At about 2:12 the Adagio espressivo returns: the strongest boundary of the movement, after the hush. Its arpeggios pass through a passage the report reads as C major, a region with no sharps in the score, before turning back to E major and a rush of running notes.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 2:12 (novelty 1.00) and 2:24 (0.96); level −29.1 dB at 2:10, then −14.0 dB at 2:15 and −16.4 dB at 2:20, where the local key reads C major (r 0.67) with 0.6 attacks per second. The score (IMSLP #51804, printed p. 99) marks Adagio espressivo and a C-major signature; Biamonti describes it moving almost at once to a fortissimo in C major, then back to E and calm. The bar is not aligned.

cues.title: The long hush
cues.text: The rush of running notes peaks near 2:35, with up to five attacks a second. It then slows and falls away to the deepest silence of the movement at 2:55. The score marks a diminuendo, a ritardando and a fermata before the opening tempo returns.
cues.evidence: Attack density is 3.4 per second at 2:30 and 5.0 at 2:35 (−14.6 dB), then 0.4 at 2:40 and 2:45; the level is −38.5 dB at 2:50 and −44.8 dB at 2:55, the quietest window of the file. The score (IMSLP #51804, printed p. 100) marks dim., ritardando and a fermata before Tempo primo; bars are not aligned.

cues.title: Tempo primo: the opening returns
cues.text: At about 3:00 the quiet opening material comes back, marked Tempo primo. Rosen hears this bar 66 to the end as a coda. A reviewer of the Naxos transfer calls the return of the opening material at 3:00 magical.
cues.evidence: Attack density returns to 3.8 per second at 3:00 straight after the −44.8 dB minimum at 2:55; boundaries at 3:02 (0.49), 3:16 (0.44) and 3:30 (0.42). The score marks Tempo primo on printed p. 100 (IMSLP #51804); the coda from bar 66 is Rosen’s reading as cited in Wikipedia; Biamonti has the calm prepare another reprise of the first element, from which the conclusion unfolds. Colin Clarke’s review (https://musicweb-international.com/classrev/2005/Mar05/Beethoven_schnable9_8110763.htm) places the return at 3:00 in the Naxos transfer, not necessarily this file; the bar is not aligned.

cues.title: Schnabel at Abbey Road
cues.text: Schnabel recorded Op. 109 for HMV in Abbey Road Studio No. 3 on 22 March 1932. Between 1932 and 1935 he made the first complete recordings of the 32 sonatas; the Op. 109 sides were issued as HMV DB 1822–24.
cues.evidence: The Naxos Historical review of 8.110763 gives the Op. 109 session, studio and DB 1822–24 (https://musicweb-international.com/classrev/2005/Mar05/Beethoven_schnable9_8110763.htm); Wikipedia’s Artur Schnabel article states the 1932–35 first complete cycle.

cues.title: A quiet close, then the next track
cues.text: The printed score ends on a held chord with a pedal-release sign. Pianists often link this movement to the Prestissimo without a break; here the sound dies away to silence by 3:50 and the Prestissimo is a separate track. Compare the quiet ending with the surge that begins the next.
cues.evidence: The report is −15.9 dB at 3:30, −20.9 dB at 3:40, −38.3 dB at 3:45 and −42.7 dB at 3:50, the end of the file. The score’s last page (IMSLP #51804, printed p. 100) ends on a chord with a fermata and a pedal-release sign; linked performance is described in Wikipedia’s Op. 109 analysis as often practised, not shown to occur in this recording.

transitions.title: The interrupted cadence resolves
transitions.how: The Vivace of bars 1–8 stops short of the expected dominant cadence in B major. The Adagio espressivo of bars 9–15 fills the gap with forte arpeggios over diminished-seventh chords, and the cadence only arrives in bar 15. Tempo I then resumes in the dominant region. The quarrel between a lyrical bagatelle and a fantasia is therefore also a delayed cadence: the second idea is the first idea’s unfinished business.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 0:34 (0.71) and another at 0:38 (0.70), after a rise in attack density to 4.0 per second at 0:30. The bar numbers and the cadence in bar 15 come from the score analysis cited in the Wikipedia Op. 109 article; no bar is aligned to this recording.

transitions.title: From loud octaves to a hush
transitions.how: The development keeps the Vivace tempo throughout. Its legato lines, sf–p accents and crescendos build to loud octaves, which the report reads as B major (the dominant of E) from about 1:25 to 1:50. The sound then falls to a hush, and the Vivace material returns in a quieter register before the second Adagio. The join is a build and a release, not a change of tempo.
transitions.evidence: The key estimate reads B major (r 0.87–0.95) at 1:25–1:50, with loud windows at 1:35 and 1:40 (−14.4 and −10.8 dB); a boundary at 1:54 (0.54) follows, and the level is −29.9 dB at 2:05. The score (IMSLP #51804, printed pp. 98–99) shows crescendos, sfp accents and loud octaves before the hush; the exact bar of the return is not aligned.

transitions.title: A hush, then the arpeggios
transitions.how: After the Vivace’s quiet return the metre changes from 2/4 to 3/4 and the tempo to Adagio espressivo. The sound leaps from a hush to forte arpeggios, and the harmony moves through a passage with no sharps in the key signature before E major returns. The same break-in of the fantasia happened at bar 9; this time it is longer, and it ends on the long hush before the coda.
transitions.evidence: Level −29.1 dB at 2:10 and −14.0 dB at 2:15; the strongest boundary is 2:12 (1.00), followed by 2:24 (0.96). The report reads C major at 2:20 (r 0.67). The score (IMSLP #51804, printed p. 99) marks Adagio espressivo in 3/4 and a signature change; bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: Ritardando, fermata, Tempo primo
transitions.how: The Adagio ends in running notes that slow in a diminuendo and a ritardando to a fermata. Silence follows, the deepest of the movement at 2:55. Tempo primo, in 2/4, then brings the quiet opening material back, as the coda that Rosen reads from bar 66. The return is a change of tempo, metre and character: the fantasia has said its last word and the bagatelle is left.
transitions.evidence: Attack density is 5.0 per second at 2:35 and 0.4 at 2:40 and 2:45; level −38.5 dB at 2:50 and −44.8 dB at 2:55, then 3.8 attacks per second at 3:00. The score (IMSLP #51804, printed p. 100) marks dim., ritardando, a fermata and Tempo primo; the coda from bar 66 is Rosen’s reading as cited in Wikipedia. Bars are not aligned.

composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
